title: Lexical relevance and keyword weighting (TF-IDF, BM25)
summary: Lexical scoring ranks documents by the query words they contain. Tf-idf gives a term more weight when it occurs many times in few documents and least when it appears in virtually all documents. BM25, described by Robertson and Zaragoza, is a term-weighting and document-scoring function with term frequency saturation and document length normalisation; the textbook describes two tuning parameters, k1 and b. Proximity can also be scored, for example by the smallest window containing all query terms. For practitioners: repeating a term has diminishing returns in BM25, and Google's spam policy defines keyword stuffing as filling a page with keywords to manipulate rankings. Papers and textbooks describe methods; none of these sources says what Google or Bing use.
actions: Write for the topic and its distinctive terms in natural language; do not set a keyword density target.
When tuning your own site search (Elasticsearch, OpenSearch), expect k1 to control term frequency scaling and b to control length normalization.
Treat repeated exact-match phrases as risk under Google's keyword stuffing definition, not as a lever.
Do not cite a textbook or paper as proof of what Google ranks on.

myths.myth: Keyword density is a ranking factor, so hit a target percentage.
myths.correction: Google's spam policy defines keyword stuffing as filling a page with keywords to manipulate rankings, and John Mueller (as reported by Search Engine Journal, secondary) said the number of times you use a keyword does not really matter or make sense. No saved source gives a target density.

myths.myth: Each extra repeat of a term keeps raising a BM25 score.
myths.correction: Robertson and Zaragoza describe a saturation point beyond which a single term's contribution cannot rise.

items.prompt: In BM25, which tuning parameter set to 0 turns off document length normalization?
items.explanation: The textbook says b = 1 fully scales the term weight by document length and b = 0 corresponds to no length normalization. The other parameter, k1, calibrates term frequency scaling, not length.

items.prompt: In tf-idf weighting, which kind of term gets the lowest weight?
options: A. A term used many times in a small number of documents
B. A term used once in a few documents
C. A term found in virtually all documents
D. A term whose idf is high
items.explanation: Correct: the textbook says the weight is lowest when the term occurs in virtually all documents. Wrong: many times in few documents is the textbook's highest-weight case. Once in only a few documents is a term that occurs fewer times in a document, which the textbook says lowers the weight but does not call the lowest case. A high idf belongs to a rare term, which gets more weight, not less.

items.prompt: True or false: in the bag of words model, the exact ordering of terms in a document is ignored but the number of occurrences of each term is material.
options: True
False
items.explanation: That is how the textbook describes the bag of words model. Order is dropped; counts are kept.

items.prompt: Which tf-idf component makes a rare query term worth more than a common one?
items.explanation: The textbook says the idf of a rare term is high and the idf of a frequent term is likely to be low. Term frequency (tf) counts occurrences inside one document; it does not look at how many documents contain the term.

items.prompt: A writer says: 'Keyword density is a ranking factor, so we aim for 3 percent.' Which statement do the saved sources support?
options: A. Google's policy treats keyword stuffing as spam
B. Google gives 2 to 3 percent as the ideal
C. Mueller said keyword counts directly set rank position
D. Google's spam policy says more repeats raise rankings
items.explanation: Correct: Google's spam policy defines keyword stuffing as filling a page with keywords to manipulate rankings. Wrong: no saved source gives an ideal density figure. Mueller, as reported by Search Engine Journal (a secondary report; no transcript was available), said: 'In general the number of times that you use a keyword on a page, I don't think that really matters or makes sense.' The spam policy says the opposite of the last option: repetition meant to manipulate rankings is the violation. Caution: the sources do not use the words 'density is not a ranking factor'.

items.prompt: Which statement is NOT supported by the textbook and review sources on BM25?
options: A. A k1 of 0 corresponds to a binary model with no term frequency
B. Setting b to 1 switches length normalization off entirely
C. BM25 caps a single term's contribution at a saturation point
D. BM25 is a term-weighting and document-scoring function
items.explanation: Unsupported: b = 1 corresponds to fully scaling the term weight by document length; b = 0 is no length normalization. The other three are supported: k1 = 0 is a binary model (textbook), term contribution cannot exceed a saturation point, and BM25 is described as a term-weighting and document-scoring function (Robertson and Zaragoza).

items.prompt: Hypothetical test index: you set BM25 k1 to 0. Page X uses 'widget' 40 times, page Y uses it once. Per the textbook, which model does k1 = 0 correspond to (one word)?
items.explanation: The textbook says a k1 value of 0 corresponds to a binary model (no term frequency), so, in the term-frequency part of the score, the 40 repeats count no differently from one occurrence.

items.prompt: Hypothetical audit note: 'BM25 caps a term's contribution, so extra repeats add little. Rare terms carry more weight than common ones. Google's spam policy sets 3 percent as the safe keyword density.' Which claim is unsupported?
options: A. BM25 caps a term's contribution at a saturation point
B. A rare term has a higher idf than a frequent term
C. Google's spam policy treats unnatural repetition as stuffing
D. Google's spam policy sets 3 percent as the safe level
items.explanation: Unsupported: the spam policy page gives no safe percentage; it defines keyword stuffing and gives repeated phrases that sound unnatural as an example. The other claims are supported by Robertson and Zaragoza (saturation), the textbook (idf) and Google's spam policy.

items.prompt: Case file (hypothetical site: Northbank Plumbing). Symptom: after a rewrite that repeated 'emergency plumber' in every paragraph to hit a 4 percent density target, the service page's rankings did not improve. Evidence: (1) the copy now reads unnaturally; (2) Google's spam policy lists 'Repeating the same words or phrases so often that it sounds unnatural' under keyword stuffing; (3) Mueller, per a Search Engine Journal report, said: 'In general the number of times that you use a keyword on a page, I don't think that really matters or makes sense.' What is the best next step?
options: A. Raise the density to 6 percent
B. Keep 4 percent and add the phrase to more headings
C. Rewrite naturally and drop the density target
D. Keep the copy and wait for the target to take effect
items.explanation: Best: both sources point away from chasing a repetition count, and the page now matches the spam policy's unnatural-repetition example. Raising density or adding more repetition moves further into that example. Waiting assumes the density target is helping, which no saved source supports. Practitioner inference: the flat rankings are not proof of cause.

items.prompt: Case file (hypothetical site: DocsCo intranet search running BM25). Symptom: long manuals fill the top 10 for generic queries while short FAQ pages sit lower. Evidence: (1) the config has b = 0; (2) k1 is unchanged; (3) the textbook says b = 1 fully scales the term weight by document length and b = 0 corresponds to no length normalization. Which change moves scoring toward length normalization?
options: A. Set k1 to 0 so the model is binary
B. Raise b toward 1 to scale by length
C. Leave b at 0 and remove idf
D. Set b to 0 so length stops mattering
items.explanation: Correct: b controls length scaling, and it is currently 0 (none). Setting k1 to 0 removes term frequency scaling, not length effects. Removing idf changes how rare terms count, unrelated to length. Setting b to 0 is what the config already has. Whether the result is better for users needs to be judged with test queries; the sources do not say.
